what.en: Today you learn the present perfect continuous (I have been working): the form English uses for an activity that started in the past and is still going on now, or that has just stopped and left traces. You will also learn when English refuses it: with state verbs like know, and when you count finished results.
what.es: Hoy aprendes el present perfect continuous (I have been working): la forma que usa el inglés para una actividad que empezó en el pasado y sigue ahora, o que acaba de parar y dejó huellas. También aprendes cuándo el inglés la rechaza: con verbos de estado como know, y cuando cuentas resultados terminados.

whyNow.en: Lesson 05 gave you have (the past touching now) and lesson 04 gave you be + -ing (an action in progress). This lesson stacks the two. It also fixes a very common calque from Spanish: "I am working here since three years."
whyNow.es: La lección 05 te dio have (el pasado que toca el ahora) y la lección 04 te dio be + -ing (una acción en progreso). Esta lección apila las dos. También corrige un calco muy común del español: "I am working here since three years."

successMeasure.es: 5 ítems nuevos en el Check, aprobar con 4/5.

term.es: Tool verb / auxiliary verb (verbo herramienta, auxiliar)

what.en: a small helper verb (have, be, do, will) that carries time or aspect instead of the main verb.
what.es: un verbo pequeño de apoyo (have, be, do, will) que carga el tiempo o el aspecto en lugar del verbo principal.

why.en: It exists because English marks most of its tenses by adding these helpers, not by changing the main verb's ending (Big Idea 4).
why.es: Existe porque el inglés marca casi todos sus tiempos agregando estos ayudantes, no cambiando la terminación del verbo principal (idea clave 4).

what.en: the verb that carries the real action (paint, wait, live).
what.es: el verbo que carga la acción real (paint, wait, live).

why.en: It exists to say what happens; in this tense it always comes last, in its -ing form.
why.es: Existe para decir qué pasa; en este tiempo siempre va de último, en su forma -ing.

what.en: the third form of a verb (worked, written, been).
what.es: la tercera forma del verbo (worked, written, been).

why.en: It exists because have always needs this form right after it: have worked, have been.
why.es: Existe porque have siempre necesita esta forma justo después: have worked, have been.

why.en: It exists to show an action from the inside, while it is moving, not as a finished block.
why.es: Existe para mostrar la acción desde adentro, mientras se mueve, no como un bloque terminado.

what.en: a verb form built with have + past participle.
what.es: una forma verbal hecha con have + participio pasado.

why.en: It exists to connect a past event or activity to the present moment (lesson 05).
why.es: Existe para conectar un evento o una actividad del pasado con el momento presente (lección 05).

what.en: a verb form built with be + -ing.
what.es: una forma verbal hecha con be + -ing.

why.en: It exists to show an action in progress at a given time (lesson 04).
why.es: Existe para mostrar una acción en progreso en un momento dado (lección 04).

what.en: a verb for a situation that doesn't move or change while it lasts (know, like, believe, own).
what.es: un verbo para una situación que no se mueve ni cambia mientras dura (know, like, believe, own).

why.en: It exists as a separate group because English treats states differently from actions: states normally refuse the -ing form.
why.es: Existe como grupo aparte porque el inglés trata los estados distinto de las acciones: los estados normalmente rechazan la forma -ing.

why.en: English marks it with for + a length of time (for three years) or since + a starting point (since 2023).
why.es: El inglés la marca con for + una cantidad de tiempo (for three years) o since + un punto de inicio (since 2023).

intro.en: The present perfect continuous looks at an activity that runs up to now.
intro.es: El present perfect continuous mira una actividad que llega hasta ahora: una actividad que empezó en el pasado y sigue (a menudo con for, since o how long); una actividad que acaba de parar y dejó evidencia ahora; una actividad temporal o repetida en las últimas semanas; y el foco en la actividad, no en el resultado (I've been painting the room: el trabajo, quizás sin terminar; I've painted the room: listo, míralo).

items.en: An activity that started in the past and is still going on, often with for, since or how long: I've been learning Swedish since March.
items.es: una actividad que empezó en el pasado y sigue (a menudo con for, since o how long)

items.en: An activity that has just stopped and left evidence now: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying? / The street is wet. It's been raining.
items.es: una actividad que acaba de parar y dejó evidencia ahora

items.en: A temporary or repeated activity in recent weeks: I've been sleeping badly lately. / She's been going to the museum every Sunday.
items.es: una actividad temporal o repetida en las últimas semanas

items.en: Focus on the activity, not the result: I've been painting the room (the work, maybe unfinished) vs. I've painted the room (done: look at it).
items.es: el foco en la actividad, no en el resultado (I've been painting the room: el trabajo, quizás sin terminar; I've painted the room: listo, míralo)

contrastPairs.es: Llevo tres años trabajando aquí. (el verbo llevar carga la duración)
contrastPairs.en: I've been working here for three years. (English has no llevar: the duration lives in have been + -ing plus for.)

contrastPairs.es: Hace dos horas que te espero. (presente: espero)
contrastPairs.en: I've been waiting for you for two hours. (English refuses the present for "time up to now": never "I wait for you since two hours.")

contrastPairs.es: Tienes los ojos rojos. ¿Estuviste llorando? (el español puede usar un pasado simple aquí)
contrastPairs.en: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying? (the evidence is here now, so English links the activity to now with have been.)

formula.en: The scene: who → have (connected to now) → been (in the middle of) → -ing (the action moving) → for/since (how long). Three verbs in a row, and each one does one job. How long questions put the question words first and then have before the subject: How long have you been living here?
formula.es: La escena: quién → have (conectado al ahora) → been (en medio de) → -ing (la acción en movimiento) → for/since (cuánto tiempo). Tres verbos seguidos, y cada uno hace un solo trabajo. En las preguntas, have pasa antes del sujeto; con how long, las palabras de pregunta van primero: How long have you been living here?

rows.affirmative: I have been working (I've been working)
rows.negative: I have not been working (I haven't been working)
rows.question: Have you been working?

rows.affirmative: She has been working (she's been working)
rows.negative: She has not been working (she hasn't been working)
rows.question: Has she been working?

contrastPairs.es: Llevo tres años estudiando. (llevar + tiempo + gerundio: el tiempo va en el medio)
contrastPairs.en: I have been studying for three years. (the three verbs stay together; the time goes at the end, after for.)

contrastPairs.es: Estudio inglés desde hace dos años. (presente + desde hace + cantidad)
contrastPairs.en: I have been studying English for two years. (for + length of time; since only takes a starting point: since 2024, never "since two years".)
How long have you been living here? (no llevar: have moves in front of the subject to make the question.)

intro.en: This lesson depends on Big Idea 4: English marks time and completion with small "tool verbs" (docs/ideas-clave.md). It also joins two lessons you already know: lesson 04 (was/were + -ing, the action in progress) and lesson 05 (have + past participle, the past connected to now).
intro.es: Esta lección depende de la idea clave 4: el inglés marca tiempo y finalización con "verbos herramienta". También une dos lecciones que ya conoces: la 04 (was/were + -ing, la acción en progreso) y la 05 (have + participio pasado, el pasado conectado con el ahora).

bigPicture.en: English doesn't change the main verb's ending to show time or completion; it plugs in tool verbs, and each tool verb does one job (Big Idea 4). Have says "this reaches now." Be + -ing says "this is in progress." When English needs both meanings at once, it doesn't invent a new ending: it uses both tools, one after the other.
bigPicture.es: El inglés no cambia la terminación del verbo principal para mostrar tiempo o finalización; conecta verbos herramienta, y cada uno hace un solo trabajo. Have dice "esto llega hasta ahora". Be + -ing dice "esto está en progreso". Cuando el inglés necesita los dos significados a la vez, no inventa una terminación nueva: usa las dos herramientas, una después de la otra.

whereItComesFrom.en: The be + -ing part most likely grew out of two rare Old and Early Middle English patterns: be + a present participle ending in -ende, and be + a preposition + a noun ending in -unge. During Middle English, sound changes merged -ende and -unge into one ending, -ing; after that, the progressive became much more common, and it reached its current form around the eighteenth century. A peer-reviewed paper on its history adds that in Old English, be + -ing mostly described a temporary state, working like an adjective; the "in progress" meaning grew stronger later. This session found no verified source for when exactly the stacked form have been + -ing first appeared, so no date is given for it here.
whereItComesFrom.es: La parte be + -ing probablemente nació de dos patrones poco comunes del inglés antiguo y del inglés medio temprano: be + un participio presente terminado en -ende, y be + una preposición + un sustantivo terminado en -unge. Durante el inglés medio, cambios de sonido fusionaron -ende y -unge en una sola terminación, -ing; después de eso, el progresivo se volvió mucho más común, y llegó a su forma actual hacia el siglo XVIII. Un artículo académico revisado por pares sobre su historia agrega que en inglés antiguo be + -ing describía sobre todo un estado temporal, funcionando como un adjetivo; el significado "en progreso" se fortaleció después. En esta sesión no se encontró una fuente verificada sobre cuándo apareció exactamente la forma apilada have been + -ing, así que aquí no se da una fecha.

problemItCreates.en: Now English has two separate tools, and neither one is enough alone. Have + past participle connects to now, but it often sounds finished: I've written the essay means it's done. Be + -ing shows something in progress, but only at one moment: I am sitting here for three hours doesn't describe the three hours behind you; it sounds like a plan for the next three hours. So how do you say "this activity started back then, has been moving the whole time, and reaches right now"?
problemItCreates.es: Ahora el inglés tiene dos herramientas separadas, y ninguna alcanza sola. Have + participio conecta con el ahora, pero muchas veces suena terminado: I've written the essay significa que ya está listo. Be + -ing muestra algo en progreso, pero solo en un momento: I am sitting here for three hours no describe las tres horas que ya pasaron; suena a un plan para las próximas tres horas. Entonces, ¿cómo dices "esta actividad empezó antes, se ha estado moviendo todo el tiempo y llega justo hasta ahora"?

englishsSolution.en: Stack the two tools: have + been + -ing. Have comes first and links to now. Because have always takes a past participle after it, be turns into been. Then the main verb comes last in its -ing form, showing the action in motion: I have been sitting here for three hours. The main verb sit never changes its ending; the tool verbs in front of it carry all the time information.
englishsSolution.es: Apilar las dos herramientas: have + been + -ing. Have va primero y conecta con el ahora. Como have siempre pide un participio pasado después, be se convierte en been. Luego el verbo principal va de último en su forma -ing, mostrando la acción en movimiento: I have been sitting here for three hours. El verbo principal sit nunca cambia su terminación; los verbos herramienta de adelante cargan toda la información de tiempo.

howNativeSpeakersSeeIt.en: A useful mental model: in lesson 04, the past continuous was a film running in the background. In lesson 05, the present perfect was a bridge from the past to now. The present perfect continuous is the film playing on the bridge: a moving clip that runs from the past right up to your feet. This is a way to picture it, not a proven fact about how native speakers think.
howNativeSpeakersSeeIt.es: Un modelo mental útil: en la lección 04, el past continuous era una película corriendo de fondo. En la lección 05, el present perfect era un puente del pasado al ahora. El present perfect continuous es la película proyectándose sobre el puente: un clip en movimiento que corre desde el pasado hasta tus pies. Es una forma de imaginarlo, no un hecho comprobado sobre cómo piensan los hablantes nativos.

spanishVsEnglish.es: Llevo tres años trabajando aquí. (un verbo especial, llevar, carga la duración)
spanishVsEnglish.en: I've been working here for three years. (dos verbos herramienta, have y been, cargan la duración)

predict.promptEn: The kitchen smells of garlic and there are pans everywhere. What has he been doing? Answer with one short sentence.
predict.why: the evidence is here now and you care about the activity, not a finished result, so you stack have + been + -ing.

predict.promptEn: Choose: "Since Monday, she ___ (has been reading / has read) four chapters of Ways of Seeing."
predict.why: four chapters counts finished units. A counted result uses the present perfect simple; the continuous is for the activity, not the count.

title.en: Also: how Spanish says it with llevar or hace... que, and why English can't copy it
title.es: También: cómo lo dice el español con llevar o hace... que, y por qué el inglés no lo puede copiar

body.en: Spanish has two everyday ways to say "this started in the past and is still going on": llevar + time + gerund (Llevo tres años trabajando aquí) and hace + time + que + present (Hace tres años que trabajo aquí), plus a third order, present + desde hace (Trabajo aquí desde hace tres años). In all three, a separate word carries the time link: llevar, hace or desde hace. That's why the Spanish main verb can stay in the simple present (trabajo). English has no separate "duration verb" like llevar: the duration has to live inside the verb form itself, and that job belongs to have. The present tense alone can't reach back; English grammars list "They know each other since January" and "They're knowing each other since January" as errors for "time up to now," and I am sitting here for three hours sounds like an intention, not a history. So a word-for-word copy of hace tres años que trabajo ("I work here since three years") breaks twice: wrong tense and wrong preposition. The same logic continues into the past: Spanish llevaba dos horas durmiendo becomes I had been sleeping for two hours (a later lesson).
body.es: El español tiene dos formas cotidianas de decir "esto empezó en el pasado y sigue": llevar + tiempo + gerundio (Llevo tres años trabajando aquí) y hace + tiempo + que + presente (Hace tres años que trabajo aquí), más un tercer orden, presente + desde hace (Trabajo aquí desde hace tres años). En las tres, una palabra aparte carga el vínculo con el tiempo: llevar, hace o desde hace. Por eso el verbo principal en español puede quedarse en presente simple (trabajo). El inglés no tiene un "verbo de duración" aparte como llevar: la duración tiene que vivir dentro de la forma verbal, y ese trabajo le toca a have. El presente solo no alcanza a mirar hacia atrás; las gramáticas de inglés marcan "They know each other since January" y "They're knowing each other since January" como errores para "tiempo hasta ahora", y I am sitting here for three hours suena a una intención, no a una historia. Por eso copiar palabra por palabra hace tres años que trabajo ("I work here since three years") falla dos veces: tiempo verbal equivocado y preposición equivocada. La misma lógica sigue en el pasado: llevaba dos horas durmiendo se vuelve I had been sleeping for two hours (una lección posterior).

title.en: Also: why I've been painting the room and I've painted the room mean different things
title.es: También: por qué I've been painting the room y I've painted the room significan cosas distintas

body.en: Both forms connect to now, but they point the camera at different things. The present perfect simple emphasises completion: I've painted the room means the job is done; come and look at the walls. The present perfect continuous emphasises the activity: I've been painting the room means that's what you've been doing; maybe it's finished, maybe not, and maybe the evidence is the paint on your hands. That's also why numbers push you to the simple form: I've painted two rooms counts finished results, and a count only makes sense for things that are complete. And verbs that happen at a single point (start, stop, finish) normally don't take the continuous here at all: Has the concert started?, not "Has the concert been starting?"
body.es: Las dos formas conectan con el ahora, pero apuntan la cámara a cosas distintas. El present perfect simple enfatiza que está terminado: I've painted the room significa que el trabajo está listo; ven a ver las paredes. El present perfect continuous enfatiza la actividad: I've been painting the room significa que eso es lo que has estado haciendo; quizás terminaste, quizás no, y quizás la evidencia es la pintura en tus manos. Por eso los números te empujan a la forma simple: I've painted two rooms cuenta resultados terminados, y contar solo tiene sentido con cosas completas. Y los verbos que pasan en un solo punto (start, stop, finish) normalmente no usan el continuo aquí: Has the concert started?, no "Has the concert been starting?"

title.en: Also: why state verbs still refuse -ing here
title.es: También: por qué los verbos de estado siguen rechazando -ing aquí

body.en: The -ing part of this tense comes from be + -ing, and that part brings its own rule with it. State verbs describe situations that stay the same the whole time they last (know, like, believe, own), and in English they normally don't take the progressive: "I am knowing the answer" is wrong (you saw this in lesson 04 with "I was knowing"). Stacking have in front doesn't change that. So for states, English uses the plain present perfect even when the situation is still going on: I've known her for years, I've been here for half an hour (never "I've been being here"). In spoken English you will sometimes hear sense verbs in the continuous for something temporary (I've been hearing strange noises outside), but know, like and believe stay simple. Interestingly, Spanish shows a similar limit: a Spanish grammar guide notes that states like saber, tener and ser generally don't fit llevar + gerund either, and Spanish prefers desde hace for them. A useful mental model for the English rule: -ing films something moving; a state has no moving parts to film.
body.es: La parte -ing de este tiempo viene de be + -ing, y esa parte trae su propia regla. Los verbos de estado describen situaciones que se mantienen iguales todo el tiempo que duran (know, like, believe, own), y en inglés normalmente no usan el progresivo: "I am knowing the answer" está mal (lo viste en la lección 04 con "I was knowing"). Poner have adelante no cambia eso. Entonces, para los estados, el inglés usa el present perfect simple aunque la situación siga: I've known her for years, I've been here for half an hour (nunca "I've been being here"). En el inglés hablado a veces vas a oír verbos de los sentidos en continuo para algo temporal (I've been hearing strange noises outside), pero know, like y believe se quedan en simple. Algo curioso: el español muestra un límite parecido. Una guía de gramática española indica que estados como saber, tener y ser en general tampoco encajan en llevar + gerundio, y el español prefiere desde hace para ellos. Un modelo mental útil para la regla del inglés: -ing filma algo que se mueve; un estado no tiene partes que se muevan para filmar.

traps.wrongEn: I am working here since three years.
traps.rightEn: I've been working here for three years.

why.en: two problems. The present continuous can't reach back over "time up to now" (it sounds like a plan), so you need have been. And since needs a starting point (since 2023); a length of time takes for.
why.es: Dos problemas. El presente continuo no alcanza a mirar el "tiempo hasta ahora" (suena a un plan), así que necesitas have been. Y since necesita un punto de inicio (since 2023); una cantidad de tiempo va con for.

traps.wrongEn: I've been knowing her for years.

why.en: know is a state verb. States refuse -ing, even inside this tense, so English uses the present perfect simple.
why.es: Know es un verbo de estado. Los estados rechazan -ing, incluso dentro de este tiempo, así que el inglés usa el present perfect simple.

traps.wrongEn: How long are you living here?
traps.rightEn: How long have you been living here?

why.en: how long up to now needs have. "How long are you living here?" sounds like a question about your plans (how long you will stay), not about the time you've already spent there.
why.es: How long hasta ahora necesita have. "How long are you living here?" suena a una pregunta sobre tus planes (cuánto tiempo te vas a quedar), no sobre el tiempo que ya llevas ahí.

traps.wrongEn: I've been writing three emails this morning.
traps.rightEn: I've written three emails this morning.

why.en: three emails counts finished results, and counts go with the simple form. The continuous works without the number: I've been writing emails all morning.
why.es: Three emails cuenta resultados terminados, y los conteos van con la forma simple. El continuo funciona sin el número: I've been writing emails all morning.

hack.en: Clock or counter? Before you speak, ask what you're looking at. If you're looking at a clock (how long, still moving, the activity itself): have been + -ing. If you're looking at a counter (how many, done, the result): have + past participle. And a state (know, like, believe) has no clock that ticks: it always takes the simple form.
hack.es: ¿Reloj o contador? Antes de hablar, pregúntate qué estás mirando. Si miras un reloj (cuánto tiempo, todavía en movimiento, la actividad en sí): have been + -ing. Si miras un contador (cuántos, terminado, el resultado): have + participio pasado. Y un estado (know, like, believe) no tiene un reloj que avance: siempre va con la forma simple.

verbList.usesEn: tool verb (perfect): I have been working. possession (a different use): I have two brushes.
tool verb (continuous), as been after have: She has been waiting. state (plain perfect): I've been here for half an hour.
activity still going on: I've been working here for three years.
activity: I've been painting the room. result: I've painted the room.
activity: I've been writing emails all morning. counted result: I've written three emails.
duration up to now: I've been waiting for you for two hours.
duration, both forms possible: I've been living here for 20 years. / I've lived here for 20 years.
in progress now vs. up to now: I am sitting here (now) vs. I have been sitting here for three hours (up to now).
recent activity with evidence: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?
duration with for: I have been studying English for two years.
state verb, no -ing: I've known her for years.
sense, simple form: Have you heard the news? spoken, temporary: I've been hearing strange noises outside.
single-point verb, no continuous here: Has the concert started?

read.themeEn: art and the psychology of attention (a short fictional first-person story)

text.en: I have been painting the same window for three months. It is the small window above my kitchen sink, and I have been standing in front of it almost every morning since June. Friends keep asking how many paintings I have finished. The honest answer is two, and I have thrown both of them away. This probably sounds like failure, but something else has been happening. I have been looking closely at things I never saw before: the light turns green around seven, the glass holds a faint reflection of the street, and a spider has been rebuilding its web in the same corner every night. The window hasn't changed. My attention has. Before this project, I believed art was about the finished object. I have known painters who work that way, and their results are beautiful. But the activity has been teaching me something the results never could: seeing is a skill, and it grows in the doing, not in the product you hang on a wall.
text.es: Llevo tres meses pintando la misma ventana. Es la ventanita encima del lavaplatos de mi cocina, y me he parado frente a ella casi todas las mañanas desde junio. Mis amigos me preguntan cuántas pinturas he terminado. La respuesta honesta es dos, y las he botado las dos. Esto probablemente suena a fracaso, pero ha estado pasando otra cosa. He estado mirando con atención cosas que nunca había visto: la luz se vuelve verde hacia las siete, el vidrio guarda un reflejo tenue de la calle, y una araña ha estado reconstruyendo su telaraña en la misma esquina todas las noches. La ventana no ha cambiado. Mi atención sí. Antes de este proyecto, creía que el arte se trataba del objeto terminado. He conocido pintores que trabajan así, y sus resultados son hermosos. Pero la actividad me ha estado enseñando algo que los resultados nunca podrían: ver es una habilidad, y crece en el hacer, no en el producto que cuelgas en una pared.

lines.en: Use have been + -ing for an activity that started in the past and runs up to now, or that just stopped and left evidence: I've been waiting for two hours.
lines.es: Usa have been + -ing para una actividad que empezó en el pasado y llega hasta ahora, o que acaba de parar y dejó evidencia: I've been waiting for two hours.

lines.en: Build it with two tool verbs stacked (have + been) and the main verb in -ing; use for + length, since + starting point.
lines.es: Se arma con dos verbos herramienta apilados (have + been) y el verbo principal en -ing; usa for + cantidad de tiempo, since + punto de inicio.

lines.en: Biggest trap: the present can't reach back. Not "I am working here since three years" but "I've been working here for three years"; and states or counts take the simple form (I've known her, I've written three emails).
lines.es: La trampa más grande: el presente no alcanza a mirar atrás. No "I am working here since three years" sino "I've been working here for three years"; y los estados o los conteos van con la forma simple (I've known her, I've written three emails).

practice.en: Use the existing exercise types from docs/dinamicas.md, never the same type twice in a row: first escena (look at a picture with visible evidence, like wet streets or paint on someone's hands, and write 3 sentences about what has been happening), then huecos (drag have/has, been, the -ing verb and for/since into the gaps), then sombra (shadow How long have you been living here? with the weak been). No new dynamic is introduced here.
practice.es: Usa los tipos de ejercicio que ya existen en docs/dinamicas.md, nunca el mismo tipo dos veces seguidas: primero escena (mira una imagen con evidencia visible, como calles mojadas o pintura en las manos de alguien, y escribe 3 frases sobre lo que ha estado pasando), luego huecos (arrastra have/has, been, el verbo en -ing y for/since a los espacios), luego sombra (repite encima How long have you been living here? con el been débil). Aquí no se introduce ninguna dinámica nueva.

items.promptEn: Fix the sentence: "We are knowing each other since university."
items.answer: We have known each other since university.
items.why: "time up to now" needs have, and know is a state verb, so it takes the present perfect simple, not -ing.

items.promptEn: Choose the correct form: "Look at your hands! ___ (Have you painted / Have you been painting)?"
items.why: the paint on the hands is evidence of a recent activity; you're asking about the activity, not a finished result.

items.promptEn: Translate the idea, don't translate word by word: "¿Cuánto tiempo llevas viviendo en Bogotá?"
items.answer: How long have you been living in Bogotá?
items.why: English has no llevar; the duration up to now lives in have been + -ing, and have moves before the subject to make the question.

items.promptEn: Choose the correct form: "This semester she ___ (has been reading / has read) five novels by Toni Morrison."
items.why: five novels counts finished results, so the present perfect simple fits.

items.promptEn: Fix the sentence: "He has been volunteering at the museum since six months."
items.answer: He has been volunteering at the museum for six months.
items.why: six months is a length of time, so it takes for; since needs a starting point (since March).

wrapUp.en: Write one line, in English, about what you used well today. For example: "Today I said 'I've been studying English for two years' instead of 'I study English since two years.'"
wrapUp.es: Escribe una línea, en inglés, sobre lo que usaste bien hoy. Por ejemplo: "Today I said 'I've been studying English for two years' instead of 'I study English since two years.'"
